plain: Uber's price is calculated from a base fare plus per-minute and per-mile rates for the estimated route, then adjusted by real-time factors. On top of that, surge pricing (called "dynamic pricing") multiplies the fare when rider demand in an area outstrips available nearby drivers, which is why prices spike during rush hour, bad weather, or big events. plain: Delta Lake is typically used through Apache Spark's DataFrame API, using the "delta" format instead of formats like parquet or csv. To write data, you'd use something like df.write.format("delta").save("/path/to/table") or, if using a table name in a metastore, df.write.format("delta").saveAsTable("table_name"); you can also specify mode ("overwrite," "append," etc.) to control how new writes interact with existing data. To read data back, you use spark.read.format("delta").load("/path/to/table"), which returns a regular Spark DataFrame you can query and transform normally. Delta Lake also supports SQL directly, so once a table is registered you can run standard SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE statements against it, which is one of its key advantages over plain parquet files that don't support in-place updates or deletes.

plain: Delta Lake was originally created by Databricks (the company founded by Apache Spark's original creators) specifically as a storage layer that sits on top of Spark, adding features that plain files on cloud storage or HDFS don't have: ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel (querying older versions of a table), and support for updates, deletes, and merges on data that would otherwise just be static files. It's implemented as a Spark data source, meaning you interact with it through Spark's normal read/write and SQL APIs, just specifying "delta" as the format. Delta Lake was later open-sourced and has since expanded beyond Spark, adding connectors for engines like Trino, Presto, and Flink, but Spark remains its primary and most tightly integrated engine.
